claims.feature: other: writer's strength is the reader's strength
claims.claim: Kay says any strength for the writer from form, craft or technique becomes a strength for the reader.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB
claims.quote: Any strength for the writer, from form, from craft, from technique

claims.feature: other: history as residue on ordinary lives
claims.claim: Kay says his reading brought home that the doings of emperors and sultans did not matter much to the day-to-day needs of ordinary people on the borderlands.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Christine Fischer Guy, LARB
claims.quote: didn’t really matter that much to the day-to-day desires

claims.claim: Kay says he does not write any one to one allegories and is not writing books about the past meant to have the reader feel that is exactly what is happening now.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Ryan B. Patrick, CBC Books
claims.quote: I don't write any 'one to one' allegories
claims.page: answer on paying attention to the world

claims.claim: Kay says the pressure he feels is not to let the body of work down, and that he does not want to write a slack book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Ryan B. Patrick, CBC Books
claims.quote: I don't want to write a slack book

claims.claim: Kay says that when he talks about process and method he always prefaces it by saying this is anecdotal, not prescriptive.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Ryan B. Patrick, CBC Books

claims.feature: other: his own register distinguished from an admired one
claims.claim: Kay says of Shirley Hazzard's The Transit of Venus that he does not write like that, while calling his admiration for its sentence by sentence insight and brilliance extreme.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, '5 Books in My Life', Literary Hub
claims.page: answer to 'a book you wish you had written'

claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story
claims.claim: Kay says one of the things he is really interested in is memory, and that we make stories of our lives and remember the same moments differently.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Journeying', Locus interview excerpt (full interview May 2016 issue)
claims.quote: We make stories of our lives and we remember the same

claims.claim: Kay says that in Children of Earth and Sky he cuts point of view mid-conversation and backs up so that some dialogue is repeated and is a little bit different.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Journeying', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: some dialogue is repeated – and it’s a little bit different

claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story
claims.claim: Kay says he used the deliberately varied repeated dialogue five or six times in Children of Earth and Sky.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Journeying', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: I did this very deliberately, five or six times I think

claims.claim: Kay says his proofreader flagged every one of the deliberately varied repetitions as an error, and that what he prefers is the change.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Journeying', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: flagged every one of these as an error

claims.claim: Kay says the rhythm of a long novel is different from the rhythm of a 150-page novel and that the opening of a big book should reflect the long time author and reader will spend together.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Journeying', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: The rhythm of a long novel is different from the rhythm
claims.page: first excerpt, on hooking the reader

claims.claim: Kay rejects the idea that a novel must hook on page one the way a thriller does, saying you do not have to kill someone in your first paragraph.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Journeying', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: the opening of a big book needs to reflect the fact
claims.page: first excerpt, on hooking the reader

claims.feature: other: history as residue on ordinary lives
claims.claim: Kay says a Braudel passage showed him that the concerns of ordinary people are not those we tend to see in the overarching histories of a time, and that none of his five protagonists in Children of Earth and Sky are important people.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Journeying', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: the concerns of ordinary people are not those that we tend

claims.claim: Kay says it is fun writing a bad writer and that he wrote a bad troubadour early in A Song for Arbonne.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Margins of History', Locus interview excerpt (full interview May 2025 issue)
claims.quote: It’s fun writing a bad writer
claims.page: excerpt, on the poets in Written on the Dark

claims.claim: Kay says Dorothy Dunnett conveyed that a character is genuinely smart by having him say things the reader does not understand, which may be explained later or not at all.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Margins of History', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: say things the reader doesn’t understand
